newsitem.title: USA: FCC denies SBC bid for long-distance service.
newsitem.headline: FCC denies SBC bid for long-distance service.

text.p: Federal phone regulators, in a precedent-setting ruling under last year's communications law, Thursday rejected SBC Communications Inc.'s bid to enter the $80 billion long-distance phone business.

The Federal Communications Commission said the San Antonio, Texas-based Baby Bell had failed to meet the law's requirement that it fully open its own local phone monopoly to competitors wanting to offer local service.
In its application to offer long-distance service from Oklahoma, SBC argued it had opened its local network in the state to competitors, such as long-distance carriers and cable-television operators.

But the FCC -- in a decision with ramifications for other regional Baby Bells -- said SBC "failed to demonstrate that there is a competing provider of telephone service to both residential and business subscribers."
The Bells have been barred from entering the lucrative long-distance market since the 1984 breakup of the old AT&T phone monopoly.

Last year's communications law gives them the opportunity if they can satisfy a 14-point federal checklist meant to generate competition in the $100 billion local phone business. But analysts said it may be months before a Bell wins clearance, given regulators' tough stance. Ameritech Corp., based in Chicago, has an application pending at the FCC.
"The power to enter the long-distance market lies in the hands of the Bell companies. If they have the will, the law makes clear the way," FCC Chairman Reed Hundt said.
But in a statement he added that SBC "plainly failed to meet the standards" spelled out under the law.
SBC called the FCC decision "a defeat for Oklahoma's consumers, for long-distance and local competition in the state, and for the Telecommunications Act of 1996 that was meant to foster competition."
SBC controls about 1.5 million phone lines in Oklahoma, one of seven states in SBC's local-calling region.
The FCC said SBC did not satisfy a number of requirements.

The agency, for example, said the carrier failed to meet the so-called "Track B" test in which a Bell can offer long-distance phoning even if no competitors have asked to hook up to the carrier's local network.

The FCC noted that SBC has received requests from rivals to link up to its network and, when implemented, such "interconnection" agreements will pave the way to the kind of competing local service required under the law. SBC says it has signed 16 interconnection pacts with rivals.
And the FCC said SBC failed to meet the 14-point check-list for opening local monopolies under last year's communications law.
The rejection comes after the Justice Department recommended last month that the FCC deny SBC's bid.
"There was very little likelihood that SBC's application was going to be approved, especially once it was opposed by the Justice Department," said attorney Scott Harris of Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher.
The department's antitrust division on Wednesday advised the FCC to reject Ameritech's application to offer long-distance calling from Michigan.
Analyst Scott Cleland said SBC may face an even tougher hurdle than other Bells, given the carrier's recent talks to merge with No. 1 long-distance phone giant AT&T Corp.

"The rumoured AT&T-SBC merger politically puts SBC at the end of the Baby Bell line for getting into long-distance," said Cleland, of Legg Mason Precursor Group, the research from of the Baltimore-based brokerage.
SBC stock rose 25 cents to $59.06 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading.
